A **confidence interval (CI)** gives a range of plausible values for an unknown population parameter, such as a population mean.

For a mean, the general form is:

$$
\text{estimate} \pm \text{margin of error}
$$

**Example:** Suppose a random sample of $100$ people has a mean of $50$ and a standard deviation of $10$.

1. Calculate the standard error: $SE = 10/\sqrt{100} = 1$.
2. For an approximate 95% CI, multiply by $1.96$: the margin of error is $1.96$.
3. Construct the interval: $50 \pm 1.96 = (48.04,\ 51.96)$.

The standard error measures sampling variability; the multiplier sets the confidence level. This approximation assumes an independent random sample and a suitable sampling distribution.

**Interpretation:** If we repeatedly sampled and built intervals this way, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true population mean.

**Takeaway:** A confidence interval combines an estimate with a margin reflecting its uncertainty.

notes.title: Confidence interval
notes.content: A confidence interval (CI) is a range of plausible values for an unknown population parameter, constructed from sample data.

notes.title: Confidence interval for a mean (approximate)
notes.content: CI = estimate ± margin of error. For a 95% CI with known/large-sample standard error, margin of error is approximately $1.96\,SE$.

notes.title: Constructing a confidence interval
notes.content: 1. Compute the standard error (e.g. $SE=s/\sqrt n$). 2. Choose the critical multiplier for the confidence level (approximately 1.96 for 95%). 3. Calculate estimate ± multiplier × SE.

notes.title: Interpreting a 95% confidence interval
notes.content: In repeated sampling, about 95% of intervals constructed by this method would contain the true population parameter; it is not a 95% probability statement about a particular fixed interval.

notes.title: 95% CI example for a mean
notes.content: With $n=100$, sample mean $50$, and sample SD $10$: $SE=10/\sqrt{100}=1$. Approximate 95% CI: $50\pm1.96=(48.04,51.96)$.
